In mathematics, the notion of ''"common limit in the range"'' property denoted by '''CLRg property'''<ref name=Wutiphol>{{Cite journal|title=Common Fixed Point Theorems for a Pair of Weakly Compatible Mappings in Fuzzy Metric Spaces|first1=Wutiphol|last1=Sintunavarat|first2=Poom|last2=Kumam|date=August 14, 2011|journal=Journal of Applied Mathematics|volume=2011|article-number=e637958|doi=10.1155/2011/637958|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=Wutiphol2>{{Cite journal|title=Common fixed points for R-weakly commuting in fuzzy metric spaces
|first1=Wutiphol |last1=Sintunavarat|first2=Poom |last2=Kumam|date=2012|journal=Annali dell'Università di Ferrara|volume=58|pages=389-406|doi=10.1007/s11565-012-0150-z|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=ravi>{{Cite journal|title=A comparison of various noncommuting conditions in metric fixed point theory and their applications|first1=Ravi|last1=P Agarwal|first2=Ravindra |last2=K Bisht|first3=Naseer |last3=Shahzad|
 date= February 13, 2014|journal=Fixed Point Theory and Applications|volume=2014|pages=1–33|doi=10.1186/1687-1812-2014-38|doi-access=free }}</ref> is a theorem that unifies, generalizes, and extends the [[contractive mapping]]s in [[fuzzy metric spaces]], where the range of the [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] does not necessarily need to be a [[Closed set|closed]] [[Closed subspace (topology)|subspace]] of a non-empty [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X</math>.

Suppose <math>X</math> is a non-empty set, and <math>d</math> is a distance metric; thus, <math>(X, d)</math> is a metric space. Now suppose we have self [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] <math>f,g : X \to X.</math> These [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] are said to fulfil '''CLRg property''' if 

<math display="block">\lim_{k \to \infty} f x_{k} = \lim_{k \to \infty} g x_{k} = gx,</math>
for some <math>x \in X.</math> 

Next, we give some examples that satisfy the '''CLRg property'''.

==Examples==
Source:<ref name=Wutiphol />
===Example 1 ===
Suppose <math>(X,d)</math> is a usual metric space, with <math>X=[0,\infty).</math> Now, if the [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] <math>f,g: X \to X</math> are defined respectively as follows:

*<math>fx = \frac{x}{4}</math>
*<math>gx = \frac{3x}{4}</math>

for all <math>x\in X.</math> Now, if the following sequence <math>\{x_k\}=\{1/k\}</math> is considered. We can see that

<math display="block">
\lim_{k\to \infty}fx_{k} = \lim_{k\to \infty}gx_{k} = g0 = 0,
</math>

thus, the [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> fulfilled the '''CLRg property'''.

Another example that shades more light to this CLRg property is given below
===Example 2 ===
Let <math>(X,d)</math> is a usual metric space, with <math>X=[0,\infty).</math> Now, if the [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] <math>f,g: X \to X</math> are defined respectively as follows:

*<math>fx = x+1</math>
*<math>gx = 2x</math>

for all <math>x\in X.</math> Now, if the following sequence <math>\{x_k\}=\{1+1/k \}</math> is considered. We can easily see that

<math display="block">
\lim_{k\to \infty}fx_{k} = \lim_{k\to \infty}gx_{k} = g1 = 2,
</math>

hence,  the [[Map (mathematics)|mappings]] <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> fulfilled the '''CLRg property'''.
